questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steady current of 1.6 A flows through a metal wire. Taking the magnitude of the electronic charge as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the number of free electrons crossing any cross-section of the wire per second is:

solution.concept: Current as rate of flow of charge: I = (number per second) × e
solution.explanation: The charge crossing a section per second is the current. Each electron carries charge e, so the number of electrons per second is I/e.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.56 × 10⁻¹⁹ multiplies I by e instead of dividing. 6.25 × 10¹⁸ is the number per second for 1 A, not 1.6 A. 1.0 × 10¹⁸ is a slip in the power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electric current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A number of identical resistors give an equivalent resistance of 50 Ω when all of them are connected in series and 2 Ω when all of them are connected in parallel. The number of resistors and the resistance of each are:

solution.concept: n identical resistors R: series nR, parallel R/n
solution.explanation: Dividing the series value by the parallel value removes R and gives n²; then R follows from nR.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 resistors takes n = R_s/R_p instead of its square root. 10 resistors of 5 Ω swaps n and R (series would then be 50 Ω but parallel 0.5 Ω). 5 resistors of 50 Ω puts the series total on each resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel
solution.final_answer: Option C: 5 resistors of 10 Ω each

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged by an external DC source, and a charging current of 4 A flows into its positive terminal. The potential difference across the terminals of the battery during charging is:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage while charging: V = ε + Ir
solution.explanation: While charging, current is driven into the positive terminal against the emf, so the external source must supply the emf and also the drop across the internal resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 V uses ε − Ir, which applies when the battery is discharging. 12 V ignores the internal resistance. 16 V adds the current (4) instead of the drop Ir (2 V).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When a potential difference is applied across a metal wire, the drift velocity of its free electrons is directed:

options.text: opposite to the direction of the electric field in the wire
along the direction of the electric field in the wire
perpendicular to the electric field in the wire
in no particular direction, since the electrons move randomly

solution.concept: Force on an electron in an electric field: F = −eE
solution.explanation: Each free electron is accelerated by the force −eE between collisions, so the average (drift) velocity it acquires is v_d = −eEτ/m, i.e. opposite to E. The conventional current is along E.
solution.why_others_wrong: Along E is the direction of conventional current, not of electron drift. Perpendicular has no basis. The thermal velocities are random, but the drift superposed on them has a definite direction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: opposite to the direction of the electric field in the wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The power dissipated in a resistor connected across a fixed potential difference V is directly proportional to its resistance.
Statement II: The commercial unit of electrical energy, 1 kilowatt-hour, is equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Electrical power P = V²/R; kilowatt-hour
solution.explanation: For a fixed V, P = V²/R, so the power is inversely proportional to R (Statement I false). 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (Statement II true).
steps: Fixed V: P = V²/R ∝ 1/R → Statement I false
1 kWh = 10³ × 3600 J = 3.6 × 10⁶ J → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: P ∝ R holds for a fixed current (P = I²R), not for a fixed potential difference; so options with Statement I true are wrong, and Statement II is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal has 6.25 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³ and a resistivity of 2.25 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Taking the electron mass as 9.0 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the average relaxation time of the free electrons is:

solution.concept: Resistivity in terms of relaxation time: ρ = m/(ne²τ)
solution.explanation: The free-electron model gives ρ = m/(ne²τ). Rearranging gives τ = m/(ne²ρ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 × 10⁻³³ s uses e instead of e². 4.0 × 10¹³ s inverts the expression. 1.25 × 10⁻¹⁴ s halves the correct value (an extra factor of 2).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf 12 V and negligible internal resistance is connected in series with a resistor R and a 4 Ω resistor. A second cell, of emf 3 V and negligible internal resistance, is connected in series with a galvanometer, and this branch is connected across the 4 Ω resistor, the positive terminal of the 3 V cell being joined to the end of the 4 Ω resistor that is at the higher potential. The galvanometer shows no deflection. The value of R is:

solution.concept: Loop rule for a branch carrying no current
solution.explanation: With no current in the galvanometer branch, the loop rule round that branch and the 4 Ω resistor gives: p.d. across 4 Ω = 3 V. The main loop then carries a current 3/4 A, which fixes R.
steps: No current in the 3 V branch → I × 4 = 3 → I = 0.75 A
Main loop: 12 = I(R + 4) → R + 4 = 16 → R = 12 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 Ω is the total resistance of the main loop, not R. 4/3 Ω inverts the ratio of the voltages (9 V across R, 3 V across 4 Ω). 9 Ω divides the 9 V across R by 1 A instead of 0.75 A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 Ω and Q = 30 Ω are in series between points A and C, meeting at B, and R = 20 Ω and S = 90 Ω are in series between A and C, meeting at D (P and R are joined at A). A cell is connected between A and C and a galvanometer between B and D. To balance the bridge without changing P, Q or R, a resistor should be connected to S as follows:

solution.concept: Balance condition P/Q = R/S; parallel combination to reduce a resistance
solution.explanation: Balance needs S_eff = RQ/P = 20 × 30/10 = 60 Ω. Since 90 Ω is too large, a resistor X must be put in parallel with S: 90X/(90 + X) = 60.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 Ω in parallel gives 22.5 Ω and 60 Ω in parallel gives 36 Ω, not 60 Ω. A resistor in series can only increase S above 90 Ω.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option D: 180 Ω in parallel with S

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric heater is rated 1000 W, 220 V. If the supply voltage falls to 200 V, the power drawn by the heater falls by about (assume its resistance stays the same):

solution.concept: P = V²/R for a fixed resistance
solution.explanation: With R fixed, P ∝ V², so the new power is (200/220)² of the rated power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9% assumes P ∝ V. 83% is the fraction of power that remains, not the fall. 21% is (220/200)² − 1, the increase computed the wrong way round.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two cells of emfs ε₁ and ε₂ and internal resistances r₁ and r₂, connected in parallel (positive terminal to positive terminal), are equivalent to a single cell of emf (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂).
Statement II: The internal resistance of this parallel combination is r₁ + r₂.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Cells in parallel
solution.explanation: For two cells in parallel, the equivalent emf is (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) (Statement I true) and the equivalent internal resistance is r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂), like two resistors in parallel (Statement II false). r₁ + r₂ is the internal resistance of the series combination.
steps: ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) → Statement I true
r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂), not r₁ + r₂ → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II gives the series result, so options with Statement II true are wrong; Statement I is the standard result, so options with it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A uniform metal wire is stretched until its length is doubled. Its volume, resistivity and temperature do not change. Match each quantity in List-I with its change in List-II.

List-I:
A. Resistance of the wire
B. Resistivity of the material
C. Cross-sectional area of the wire
D. Current density, for the same current through the wire

List-II:
I. Unchanged
II. Becomes 4 times
III. Becomes half
IV. Becomes twice

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with constant volume; resistivity is a material property; J = I/A
solution.explanation: Constant volume means A halves when l doubles. Then R = ρl/A becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times. Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature, so it is unchanged. For the same current, J = I/A doubles.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV takes R ∝ l only and forgets that A also halves. B-IV treats resistivity as if it changed with shape. C-IV makes the area double instead of halve.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about combinations of resistors are correct?

(a) In a parallel combination, the current through each resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance.
(b) The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is less than the smallest of the individual resistances.
(c) The equivalent resistance of a series combination is greater than the largest of the individual resistances.
(d) Connecting one more resistor in parallel with an existing parallel combination increases its equivalent resistance.
(e) In a series combination, the potential difference across each resistor is proportional to its resistance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series and parallel combinations
solution.explanation: In parallel all resistors have the same V, so I = V/R ∝ 1/R, and 1/R_eq = Σ1/R is larger than any single 1/R, making R_eq smaller than the smallest R. Adding a branch adds to 1/R_eq, so R_eq decreases. In series the same current flows, so V = IR ∝ R and R_eq = ΣR exceeds the largest R.
steps: (d) adding a parallel branch lowers R_eq: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (e). The other two options include (d), which is false, or leave out true statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are used to send a current through an external resistor R. The current in R is found to be the same whether the four cells are all connected in series or all connected in parallel. The current in R is:

solution.concept: Series: nε/(R + nr); parallel: ε/(R + r/n)
solution.explanation: Equating the two currents fixes R; then either expression gives the current.
steps: nε/(R + nr) = ε/(R + r/n) → n(R + r/n) = R + nr → (n − 1)R = (n − 1)r → R = r = 0.5 Ω
solution.shortcut: The two groupings give equal currents exactly when R equals the internal resistance of one cell.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 A takes R = 0 in the series formula. 0.6 A uses the emf of one cell with the internal resistance of all four in series. 1.2 A halves the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Five resistors are connected between points A and B as follows: 2 Ω from A to C, 4 Ω from C to B, 3 Ω from A to D, 6 Ω from D to B, and 5 Ω between C and D. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:

solution.concept: Balanced Wheatstone bridge: the middle resistor carries no current
solution.explanation: The four outer resistors form a Wheatstone bridge with ratio 2/4 = 3/6, so C and D are at the same potential whatever voltage is applied between A and B. The 5 Ω resistor carries no current and can be removed.
steps: Path ACB = 6 Ω, path ADB = 9 Ω
solution.shortcut: Check P/Q = R/S first; if it holds, drop the bridging resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.1 Ω treats the 5 Ω resistor as if it were connected in parallel across A and B. 5.0 Ω is just the bridging resistor. 20 Ω adds all five resistors in series.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two heater coils, each connected separately across the same mains supply, boil a given quantity of water in 10 minutes and 15 minutes respectively. If the two coils are connected in parallel across the same supply, the time taken to boil the same quantity of water is (neglect heat losses and any change of resistance):

solution.concept: Heat H = (V²/R)t at fixed V; parallel powers add
solution.explanation: The same heat H is needed each time. With V fixed, P = V²/R, so t = H/P ∝ R. In parallel the powers add: P = P₁ + P₂, so 1/t = 1/t₁ + 1/t₂.
solution.shortcut: Parallel: t = t₁t₂/(t₁ + t₂); series: t = t₁ + t₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 minutes is the time with the coils in series. 12.5 minutes is the average of the two times. 5 minutes would need the two times to be equal (10 and 10).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A resistor R₁ is connected in series with a resistor R₂ across a battery. A voltmeter of finite resistance, connected across R₁, reads less than the potential difference that existed across R₁ before the voltmeter was connected.
Reason (R): The voltmeter in parallel with R₁ lowers the resistance of that part of the circuit, so this part takes a smaller share of the battery voltage.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Loading effect of a voltmeter; potential divider
solution.explanation: In a series circuit the voltage divides in proportion to the resistances. The voltmeter (resistance R_V) in parallel with R₁ makes that part R₁R_V/(R₁ + R_V) < R₁, while R₂ (and any internal resistance) is unchanged, so the share of the voltage across that part falls. This is exactly why the reading is low; an ideal voltmeter would need infinite resistance.
steps: Smaller fraction of the battery voltage across it → reading low (A true)
R states this mechanism → R true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the actual cause of the lower reading, so option B is wrong; both statements are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A uniform metal wire is connected across an ideal battery of constant emf. It is replaced by a wire of the same material and the same length but twice the diameter, connected across the same battery. The temperature of the wire is the same in both cases. Which of the following statements are correct for the second wire, compared with the first?

(a) The current through it is four times as large.
(b) The drift speed of its free electrons is the same.
(c) The electric field inside it is the same.
(d) The power dissipated in it is four times as large.
(e) The resistivity of its material is one-fourth as large.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A; I = neAv_d; E = V/l; P = V²/R
solution.explanation: Doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times, so R becomes one-fourth and I = V/R becomes 4 times. The field E = V/l is unchanged because V and l are unchanged, so v_d = (eτ/m)E is unchanged (check: v_d = I/(neA) = 4I/(ne·4A)). P = V²/R becomes 4 times. Resistivity depends on material and temperature only, so it is unchanged.
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (d) only and (b), (c) and (d) only leave out true statements. (a), (c) and (e) only includes (e), which is false because resistivity does not depend on the dimensions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: In the definition of the ampere based on the force between currents, one ampere is the steady current which, maintained in each of two very long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces on each conductor a force of:

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents: f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
solution.explanation: With I₁ = I₂ = 1 A and d = 1 m, f = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1 × 1)/(2π × 1) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre. This is the basis of the definition of the ampere given in the textbook.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4π × 10⁻⁷ is µ₀ itself, forgetting the 2π in the denominator. 1 × 10⁻⁷ is µ₀/4π. 1 N/m has no basis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force between two parallel currents, the ampere
solution.final_answer: Option A: 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A moving-coil galvanometer has a current sensitivity of 10 divisions per mA and a coil resistance of 20 Ω. Its voltage sensitivity is:

solution.concept: Voltage sensitivity = current sensitivity / G
solution.explanation: A potential difference V drives a current V/G through the coil, so the deflection per unit voltage is the deflection per unit current divided by G.
steps: = 0.5 division per (mA × Ω) = 0.5 division per mV
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 divisions per mV multiplies by G. 2 divisions per mV inverts the ratio (G/I_s). 0.05 division per mV is a slip of a factor of 10.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A short bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 0.5 A m². Taking µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ignoring all other magnetic fields, the magnitude of its magnetic field at a point on its equatorial line (the perpendicular bisector of its axis), 10 cm from its centre, is:

solution.concept: Equatorial field of a short magnet: B = µ₀m/(4πr³)
solution.explanation: On the equatorial line of a short dipole the field is (µ₀/4π)(m/r³), half of the axial field at the same distance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10⁻⁴ T is the axial value (2m/r³). 5 × 10⁻⁶ T divides by r² instead of r³. 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T halves the equatorial value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Which one of the following substances is ferromagnetic at room temperature?

solution.concept: Classification of magnetic materials
solution.explanation: Iron, cobalt, nickel and gadolinium are the common ferromagnetic substances. Copper and water are diamagnetic; aluminium is paramagnetic.
steps: Ferromagnetic examples: Fe, Co, Ni, Gd → nickel
solution.why_others_wrong: Copper and water are diamagnetic and aluminium is paramagnetic; none of them is ferromagnetic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Three long straight wires are perpendicular to the plane of a closed loop. Wire 1 carries 5 A out of the plane and wire 2 carries 2 A into the plane; both pass through the region enclosed by the loop. Wire 3 carries 6 A out of the plane and lies outside the loop. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the line integral of the magnetic field round the loop, ∮B·dl, is about:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = µ₀I_enclosed (algebraic sum)
solution.explanation: Only currents that pass through the surface bounded by the loop count, with opposite directions taking opposite signs. Wire 3, outside the loop, contributes nothing to the line integral (though it does contribute to B at points of the loop).
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.8 × 10⁻⁶ T m adds 5 A and 2 A ignoring their directions. 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ T m also counts the 6 A wire outside the loop. Zero would need the enclosed currents to cancel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long straight parallel wires, 10 cm apart, carry currents of 5 A each in opposite directions. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the point midway between the wires is:

solution.concept: Field of a long wire B = µ₀I/(2πd); superposition
solution.explanation: Between two wires with opposite currents, the fields of the two wires point the same way (use the right-hand rule on each), so they add. Each wire is 5 cm from the midpoint.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero is the result for currents in the same direction. 2 × 10⁻⁵ T uses 10 cm instead of 5 cm for the distance. 1 × 10⁻⁵ T is one wire at 10 cm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law (field of a long straight wire)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long horizontal straight wire has a mass of 50 g per metre of its length. It is held in mid-air, with no support, by a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.5 T at right angles to the wire. Taking g = 10 m/s², the current in the wire is:

solution.concept: Force on a current: F = BIl; balance with weight
solution.explanation: For the wire to float, the upward magnetic force on each metre must equal the weight of each metre: BI × 1 = (mass per metre) × g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 A leaves out g. 10 A divides B by the mass per metre (an inverted ratio). 0.25 A multiplies by B instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle of radius 10 cm at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. Its kinetic energy is:

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB) → p = qBr; K = p²/(2m)
solution.explanation: The radius fixes the momentum: p = qBr. The kinetic energy follows from K = p²/2m and is converted to eV by dividing by e.
solution.why_others_wrong: 250 keV uses K = p²/m (no factor ½). 62.5 keV halves the answer again. 12.5 keV is a slip of a factor of 10.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In an unmagnetised piece of ferromagnetic material, the domains are oriented at random, so that the net magnetisation of the piece is zero.
Statement II: When the piece is placed in an external magnetic field, the domains oriented along the field grow in size and the others tend to turn towards the field.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Domain picture of ferromagnetism
solution.explanation: Each domain is magnetised to saturation, but in an unmagnetised sample the domain magnetisations point in random directions and cancel. An external field makes domains aligned with it grow and others rotate towards it, producing a large net magnetisation along the field.
steps: Random domains → net M = 0 → Statement I true
Field → aligned domains grow, others rotate → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A flat coil of 10 turns, each of area 0.01 m², carries a current of 2 A and is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I:
A. Magnetic moment of the coil
B. Torque on the coil when its magnetic moment is perpendicular to the field
C. Potential energy of the coil when its magnetic moment is parallel to the field
D. Work done by an external agent to turn the coil slowly from the parallel to the antiparallel position

List-II:
I. 0.1 N m
II. −0.1 J
III. 0.2 J
IV. 0.2 A m²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: m = NIA; τ = mB sin θ; U = −mB cos θ; W = U_final − U_initial
solution.explanation: m = 10 × 2 × 0.01 = 0.2 A m². The torque is largest, mB = 0.1 N m, at θ = 90°. U = −mB = −0.1 J at θ = 0. Turning to θ = 180° raises U to +0.1 J, so the work needed is 0.2 J.
steps: A: m = NIA = 0.2 A m² → IV
B: τ = mB = 0.1 N m → I
solution.why_others_wrong: B-III gives the torque the value 2mB. C-III with D-II gives the potential energy and the work each other's values. A-III gives the magnetic moment the unit of work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on current loop, magnetic dipole
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Two long, straight, parallel wires carry steady currents. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If the currents are in the same direction, the wires attract each other.
(b) If the currents are in opposite directions, the wires repel each other.
(c) The force per unit length between them is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
(d) The forces the two wires exert on each other are equal in magnitude even when the currents are unequal.
(e) The wire carrying the larger current experiences the larger force.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents: f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
solution.explanation: Parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel. f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) varies as 1/d, not 1/d². The expression is symmetric in I₁ and I₂, so each wire feels the same force (Newton's third law).
steps: (d) f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) on each wire: true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) are wrong: the force falls off as 1/d and is the same on both wires.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force between two parallel currents, the ampere

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A magnetic field can change the direction of motion of a charged particle but cannot change its speed.
Reason (R): The magnetic force on a moving charged particle is always perpendicular to its velocity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Lorentz magnetic force F = q(v × B)
solution.explanation: Since F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to v, it has no component along the velocity. It can only bend the path; the speed (and kinetic energy) stays the same. R is therefore the reason for A.
steps: No force component along v → speed unchanged, direction changes → A true and follows from R
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly why the speed cannot change, so option B is wrong; both are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T fills the whole region on one side of a plane boundary and is parallel to the boundary. A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters the field region with a speed of 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s, moving perpendicular to the boundary and perpendicular to the field. The distance between the points where it enters and leaves the field region, and the time it spends in the field, are:

solution.concept: Circular motion in B: r = mv/(qB), T = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: Entering at right angles to the boundary, the proton describes a semicircle and leaves at right angles, a diameter away from the entry point, after half a period.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.10 m is the radius, not the diameter. 2π × 10⁻⁷ s is a full period; the proton completes only half a circle before leaving.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option B: 0.20 m and π × 10⁻⁷ s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long, straight, insulated wires lie in the x-y plane, one along the x-axis carrying 6 A in the +x direction and the other along the y-axis carrying 2 A in the +y direction; they cross at the origin. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field at the point (2 cm, 2 cm, 0) is:

solution.concept: B = µ₀I/(2πd) with direction from the right-hand rule; superposition
solution.explanation: Each wire is 2 cm from the point. The x-axis current (+x) produces a field along +z at a point on the +y side. The y-axis current (+y) produces a field along −z at a point on the +x side. The fields are along the same line but opposite, so they subtract.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 × 10⁻⁵ T adds the two fields as if they were in the same direction. −z gives the direction of the weaker field. 6.3 × 10⁻⁵ T treats the fields as perpendicular vectors; both are actually perpendicular to the plane.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Biot-Savart law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A wire of fixed length carries a fixed current. It is bent first into a single circular turn and then into a single square turn. The ratio of the magnetic moment of the circular turn to that of the square turn is:

solution.concept: Magnetic moment of a current loop m = IA
solution.explanation: For the same length L, the circle has radius L/(2π) and area L²/(4π); the square has side L/4 and area L²/16. With the same current, the moments are in the ratio of the areas.
solution.shortcut: For a given perimeter the circle encloses the largest area, so the ratio must exceed 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: π : 4 inverts the ratio and would make the square's moment larger. 1 : 1 ignores the different areas. 2 : π uses the wrong area for one shape.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a charged particle passes through a region of space without any deflection, the magnetic field in that region must be zero.
Reason (R): The magnetic force on a charged particle moving parallel to the magnetic field is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conditions for zero magnetic force
solution.explanation: F = q(v × B) is zero when v is parallel or antiparallel to B, so a particle can cross a non-zero magnetic field undeflected (R true). Undeflected motion is also possible when an electric force balances the magnetic force, as in crossed fields. So no deflection does not mean B = 0 (A false).
steps: v ∥ B → v × B = 0 → R true
Undeflected motion possible with B ≠ 0 → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C, which need A to be true, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A proton and an electron enter the same uniform magnetic field with equal speeds, each moving at right angles to the field. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The radius of the proton's circular path is larger than that of the electron's.
(b) The proton takes longer than the electron to complete one revolution.
(c) The proton and the electron go round their circles in opposite senses.
(d) The magnitudes of the magnetic forces on the proton and the electron are equal.
(e) The kinetic energy of each particle increases while it moves in the field.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB), T = 2πm/(qB), F = qvB; the magnetic force does no work
solution.explanation: Both have the same |q|, v and B. So F = |q|vB is the same for both. r and T are proportional to m, and the proton is about 1836 times heavier, so both are larger for the proton. Opposite charges are bent in opposite senses. The magnetic force is perpendicular to v, so kinetic energies stay constant.
steps: (e) no work done → KE constant: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (d). The other options include (e), which is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alternating current i = 2 sin ωt (in amperes) flows through a 100 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated in the resistor is:

solution.concept: Average power in a resistor: P = I_rms²R = I₀²R/2
solution.explanation: The average of sin²ωt over a cycle is ½, so the average power is half the peak power I₀²R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 W is the peak power I₀²R. 100 W takes I_rms = I₀/2. 283 W multiplies the peak voltage by the rms current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is 0.5 H. The current in one coil rises steadily from 0 to 4 A in 0.02 s. The magnitude of the emf induced in the other coil is:

solution.concept: Mutual induction: ε₂ = M dI₁/dt
solution.explanation: The emf in the second coil equals the mutual inductance times the rate of change of current in the first.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 V is MΔI, leaving out the time. 50 V halves the answer. 400 V divides by M instead of multiplying.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', mutual inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which one of the following does NOT make use of eddy currents?

options.text: Magnetic braking in some electric trains
The heating element of an electric iron
An induction furnace used to melt metals

solution.concept: Applications of eddy currents
solution.explanation: Magnetic braking, electromagnetic damping and induction furnaces all depend on currents induced in bulk metal by a changing magnetic flux. The heating element of an iron is heated by the current supplied to it through its terminals (Joule heating), not by induction.
steps: Braking, damping, induction furnace → eddy currents
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are standard applications of eddy currents listed in the textbook.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', eddy currents
solution.final_answer: Option C: The heating element of an electric iron

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each description in List-I with the law or phenomenon in List-II.

List-I:
A. The rule that gives the direction of the induced current
B. The law that gives the magnitude of the induced emf as the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
C. Emf induced in a coil by a change of current in the same coil
D. Emf induced in a coil by a change of current in a neighbouring coil

List-II:
I. Mutual induction
II. Lenz's law
III. Self-induction
IV. Faraday's law of induction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, self- and mutual induction
solution.explanation: Faraday's law gives the magnitude ε = −dΦ/dt (with N turns, −N dΦ/dt); Lenz's law fixes the direction (the minus sign). A coil's own changing current induces an emf in it (self-induction); a neighbour's changing current induces one by mutual induction.
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes with A-IV and B-II swap Faraday's and Lenz's laws. Codes with C-I and D-III swap self- and mutual induction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law, Lenz's law, inductance
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil of 500 turns carries a steady current of 2.0 A, and the magnetic flux through each of its turns is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. The self-inductance of the coil is:

solution.concept: Self-inductance from flux linkage: NΦ = LI
solution.explanation: The total flux linked with the coil is N times the flux through one turn, and L is the flux linkage per unit current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 mH leaves out the number of turns. 200 mH multiplies the flux linkage by I instead of dividing. 100 mH is the flux linkage itself, forgetting to divide by I.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a 220 V AC supply and draws a current of 5.0 A. The secondary voltage is 330 V. If the efficiency of the transformer (output power/input power) is 90%, the current in the secondary is:

solution.concept: Power balance in a transformer with losses
solution.explanation: Input power = V_pI_p. Only 90% of it appears at the output, and the output power is V_sI_s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.3 A treats the transformer as ideal (100% efficient). 2.7 A applies the 90% twice. 7.5 A uses I_s/I_p = V_s/V_p, the inverse of the correct relation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An AC generator produces an emf of peak value 200 V and frequency 50 Hz. If the speed of rotation of its coil is doubled, everything else being unchanged, the peak emf and the frequency become:

solution.concept: Generator emf ε = NBAω sin ωt
solution.explanation: Both the peak emf NBAω and the frequency ω/2π are proportional to the angular speed of the coil, so doubling the speed doubles both.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 V and 100 Hz forgets that the peak emf contains ω. 400 V and 50 Hz forgets that the frequency is set by the rotation. 800 V treats the peak emf as proportional to ω².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.5 H varies with time as i = 3t², where i is in amperes and t in seconds. The magnitude of the self-induced emf in the coil at t = 4 s is:

solution.concept: Self-induced emf ε = L di/dt
solution.explanation: The emf depends on the instantaneous rate of change of the current, found by differentiating i(t).
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 V multiplies L by the current (48 A) instead of its rate of change. 6 V uses the average rate i/t. 3 V uses the coefficient 6 without the factor t.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A metal plate swinging between the poles of a magnet is damped by eddy currents, and cutting slots in the plate reduces this damping.
Statement II: Induction furnaces use the heat produced by large eddy currents to melt metals.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Eddy currents: damping and heating
solution.explanation: Eddy currents induced in the swinging plate oppose its motion (Lenz's law). Slots break up the paths available for the currents, so the currents and the damping are much smaller. In an induction furnace a high-frequency alternating field induces large eddy currents in the metal, whose Joule heating melts it.
steps: Slots reduce the area for eddy currents → less damping → Statement I true
Induction furnace → eddy-current heating → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', eddy currents
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil draws a current of 2.0 A when connected to a 100 V DC supply, and a current of 1.0 A (rms) when connected to a 100 V (rms), 50 Hz AC supply. The self-inductance of the coil is about:

solution.concept: A coil = resistance R in series with inductance L; Z = √(R² + X_L²)
solution.explanation: On DC (steady current) the inductance plays no part, so the DC data give R. The AC data give the impedance; the inductive reactance is the remaining part, and L = X_L/(2πf).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.32 H takes the whole impedance as the reactance. 0.16 H divides the resistance by ω. 0.55 H uses ω = 50π instead of 100π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit, impedance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A bulb rated 50 W, 100 V is to be operated at its rated values from a 200 V (rms), 50 Hz AC supply by connecting a capacitor in series with it. Treating the bulb as a pure resistance, the capacitance needed is about:

solution.concept: Series RC circuit: V² = V_R² + V_C²; X_C = 1/(2πfC)
solution.explanation: At its rating the bulb takes I = P/V = 0.5 A with 100 V across it. In a series RC circuit the voltages across R and C are 90° out of phase, so they add as perpendicular phasors, not arithmetically.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.9 µF subtracts the voltages arithmetically (V_C = 100 V). 18.4 µF and 4.6 µF are off by a factor of 2 (using 2X_C or X_C/2).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a capacitor; series circuits

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An ideal capacitor is connected in a circuit. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In the steady state it blocks a steady direct current but allows an alternating current to flow in the circuit.
(b) Its reactance decreases as the frequency of the AC source increases.
(c) The average power it consumes over a complete cycle of an AC source is zero.
(d) When it is connected alone across an AC source, the current lags behind the voltage by π/2.
(e) For a steady DC source (zero frequency), its reactance is infinite.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Capacitor in AC: X_C = 1/(ωC); current leads by π/2
solution.explanation: X_C = 1/(ωC) falls as ω rises and becomes infinite at ω = 0, so DC is blocked once the capacitor is charged while AC keeps charging and discharging it. In a purely capacitive circuit the current leads the voltage by π/2, so the average power V_rmsI_rms cos 90° is zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (e). The other options include (d), which is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the magnetic flux through a closed coil is zero at some instant, the emf induced in the coil at that instant must also be zero.
Reason (R): The induced emf depends on the rate of change of the magnetic flux, not on the value of the flux at that instant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Faraday's law ε = −dΦ/dt
solution.explanation: The emf is set by dΦ/dt. In an AC generator, the flux through the coil is zero when its plane is parallel to the field, yet that is exactly when the flux is changing fastest and the emf is maximum. So A is false and R is true.
steps: Φ = 0 with dΦ/dt ≠ 0 (coil plane parallel to B in a generator) → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C, which need A to be true, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following lists parts of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?

solution.concept: Order of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution.explanation: In order of decreasing wavelength (increasing frequency) the spectrum runs: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
steps: Increasing frequency: radio < micro < IR < visible < UV < X < γ
solution.why_others_wrong: The first wrong option swaps radio waves with microwaves and UV with IR. The third is in decreasing order. The fourth puts infrared below microwaves.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option D: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Most of the ultraviolet radiation from the Sun is absorbed by the ozone layer in the atmosphere.
Reason (R): Ultraviolet radiation has longer wavelengths than visible light.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ultraviolet rays
solution.explanation: The ozone layer high in the atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation, protecting us (A true). Ultraviolet lies beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, so its wavelengths (about 400 nm down to about 1 nm) are shorter than those of visible light (R false).
steps: Ozone absorbs most solar UV → A true
UV wavelength < visible wavelength → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so options A, B and D, which need R to be true, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum - ultraviolet rays
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each part of the electromagnetic spectrum in List-I with a way in which it is produced (List-II).

List-I:
A. Radio waves
B. Infrared waves
C. X-rays
D. Gamma rays

List-II:
I. Emitted by atomic nuclei, for example in nuclear reactions
II. Accelerated motion of charges in conducting wires
III. Bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons
IV. Hot bodies and molecules

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Sources of the different parts of the EM spectrum
solution.explanation: Radio waves are produced by accelerated charges in conducting wires (antennas). Infrared is emitted by hot bodies and molecules. X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons strike a metal target. Gamma rays come from atomic nuclei.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping III and IV gives infrared the X-ray tube. A-IV puts radio waves with hot bodies. C-I with D-III swaps the sources of X-rays and gamma rays.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A charge moving with a constant velocity radiates electromagnetic waves.
Statement II: A charge oscillating with some frequency produces electromagnetic waves of the same frequency.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Sources of electromagnetic waves: accelerated charges
solution.explanation: A stationary charge produces only an electric field and a uniformly moving charge produces steady fields; neither radiates (Statement I false). An accelerated charge radiates, and an oscillating charge produces an electromagnetic wave whose frequency equals its frequency of oscillation (Statement II true).
steps: Constant velocity → no radiation → Statement I false
Oscillating charge → EM wave of the same frequency → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false, so options A and C are wrong; Statement II is true, so option B is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', sources of electromagnetic waves
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 10 µF parallel-plate capacitor is connected to an AC source, and the potential difference between its plates is v = 100 sin(1000t), with v in volts and t in seconds. The maximum value of the displacement current between the plates is:

solution.concept: Displacement current i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = C dV/dt
solution.explanation: Between the plates Φ_E = q/ε₀ = CV/ε₀, so i_d = C dV/dt, equal to the conduction current in the wires.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻³ A is CV₀, leaving out ω. 0.71 A is the rms value, not the maximum. 0.16 A divides by 2π, treating 1000 as a frequency in Hz instead of an angular frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum is E = 30 sin(2.0 × 10⁷ z − ωt) ĵ V/m, with z in metres and t in seconds. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the angular frequency ω and the magnetic field of the wave are:

options.text: ω = 6 × 10¹⁵ rad/s; B has amplitude 1 × 10⁻⁷ T and oscillates along the z-axis
ω = 6 × 10¹⁵ rad/s; B has amplitude 1 × 10⁻⁷ T and oscillates along the x-axis
ω = 6.7 × 10⁻² rad/s; B has amplitude 1 × 10⁻⁷ T and oscillates along the x-axis
ω = 6 × 10¹⁵ rad/s; B has amplitude 9 × 10⁹ T and oscillates along the x-axis

solution.concept: Plane EM wave: ω = ck, B₀ = E₀/c, E ⊥ B ⊥ direction of propagation
solution.explanation: The phase (kz − ωt) shows the wave travels along +z with k = 2.0 × 10⁷ rad/m. In vacuum ω = ck and B₀ = E₀/c. B is perpendicular to both E (along y) and the direction of travel (z), so it lies along the x-axis; E × B must point along +z, so B is along −x when E is along +y.
steps: B ⊥ ĵ and ⊥ k̂ → along the x-axis
solution.why_others_wrong: B along the z-axis would be along the direction of propagation; EM waves are transverse. 6.7 × 10⁻² rad/s uses ω = k/c. 9 × 10⁹ T multiplies E₀ by c instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves
solution.final_answer: Option B: ω = 6 × 10¹⁵ rad/s; B has amplitude 1 × 10⁻⁷ T and oscillates along the x-axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image of the same size as the object when the object is placed 40 cm in front of the mirror. The focal length of the mirror is:

solution.concept: Image at the centre of curvature; f = R/2
solution.explanation: A concave mirror gives a real image of the same size only when the object is at the centre of curvature; the image is then also at C. So R = 40 cm and f = R/2.
steps: Same-size real image → object at C → R = 40 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 cm is the radius of curvature, not the focal length. 10 cm and 80 cm are off by further factors of 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 500 nm, the path difference between the waves reaching a point P on the screen from the two slits is 1.5 µm. The point P lies on:

options.text: the third dark fringe from the central bright fringe
the sixth bright fringe from the central bright fringe
the fourth dark fringe from the central bright fringe
the third bright fringe from the central bright fringe

solution.concept: Bright fringe: path difference = nλ
solution.explanation: Constructive interference occurs where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths; n counts the bright fringes from the central one (n = 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: A dark fringe needs an odd number of half wavelengths, (n − ½)λ, but 1.5 µm is a whole number of wavelengths. 'Sixth bright fringe' divides by λ/2 instead of λ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment
solution.final_answer: Option D: the third bright fringe from the central bright fringe

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wavefront is best described as:

options.text: a surface on which all points oscillate in the same phase (a surface of constant phase)
a surface on which the amplitude of the wave is zero
the path along which the light energy travels
the surface that separates two transparent media

solution.concept: Definition of a wavefront
solution.explanation: When a disturbance spreads from a source, the locus of points that oscillate in phase is a wavefront: a surface of constant phase. The energy travels along rays, which are perpendicular to the wavefronts.
steps: Wavefront = locus of points in the same phase
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero-amplitude surfaces are not wavefronts. The path of energy is a ray, not a wavefront. A boundary between media is an interface.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle
solution.final_answer: Option A: a surface on which all points oscillate in the same phase (a surface of constant phase)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Cassegrain reflecting telescope, the light reflected by the concave primary (objective) mirror is reflected back through a hole in the primary mirror to the eyepiece by:

options.text: a plane mirror inclined at 45° to the axis
a convex lens placed at the focus of the primary

solution.concept: Reflecting telescopes: the Cassegrain arrangement
solution.explanation: In the Cassegrain design a convex secondary mirror reflects the converging light back through a hole in the primary mirror, so the image is formed behind the primary where the eyepiece and observer can be placed.
steps: Cassegrain: concave primary + convex secondary, light through a hole in the primary
solution.why_others_wrong: A plane mirror at 45° sends the light sideways (the Newtonian arrangement), not back through the primary. The secondary of a Cassegrain telescope is convex, not concave, and it is a mirror, not a lens.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments - telescope
solution.final_answer: Option B: a convex secondary mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The refractive indices of glass and water with respect to air are 3/2 and 4/3 respectively. The refractive index of glass with respect to water is:

solution.concept: Relative refractive index n₂₁ = n₂/n₁
solution.explanation: The refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is the ratio of their refractive indices (with respect to vacuum or air): n_gw = n_g/n_w.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8/9 is the refractive index of water with respect to glass. 1/6 subtracts the indices. 2 multiplies them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A simple microscope consists of a convex lens of focal length 5 cm. When the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision (25 cm), its magnifying power is:

solution.concept: Simple microscope with image at the near point: m = 1 + D/f
solution.explanation: With the image at the near point D, the angular magnification is 1 + D/f; with the image at infinity it is D/f.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is the magnifying power with the final image at infinity. 4 uses D/f − 1. 0.2 inverts D/f.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments - the microscope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a spherical mirror of small aperture, the focal length is half the radius of curvature.
Statement II: A concave mirror forms a virtual image of a real object only when the object lies between its focus and its pole.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: f = R/2; images formed by a concave mirror
solution.explanation: For paraxial rays a spherical mirror has f = R/2 (Statement I true). For a concave mirror, a real object beyond F gives a real image (at infinity when the object is at F); only an object between F and P gives a virtual, erect, magnified image (Statement II true).
steps: Virtual image only for object between P and F → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms a virtual, erect image three times the size of an object placed in front of it. The distance of the object from the mirror is:

solution.concept: Mirror formula with magnification m = −v/u
solution.explanation: A virtual erect image has m = +3, so v = −3u (image behind the mirror). Substituting in the mirror formula gives u.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm gives a real, inverted image of magnification −3 (v = −60 cm). 5 cm gives magnification 1.5. 45 cm multiplies the focal length by 3.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', mirror equation, magnification

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin equiconvex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. It is cut into two identical halves by a plane perpendicular to its principal axis, passing through its optical centre, so that each half is a plano-convex lens. The focal length of each half is:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: For the equiconvex lens both surfaces contribute equally: 1/f = (n − 1)(2/R). Each plano-convex half keeps only one curved surface (the other is plane, 1/R = 0), so its power is half.
solution.shortcut: Two halves in contact rebuild the lens: P = P₁ + P₂ → each half has half the power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm would be the answer if the lens were cut along the principal axis (each half keeps both curved surfaces). 10 cm doubles the power instead of halving it. 80 cm halves it twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens, lens maker's formula

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 650 nm falls normally on a single slit. The first minimum of the diffraction pattern is observed at an angle of 30° from the central direction. The width of the slit is:

solution.concept: First minimum of single-slit diffraction: a sin θ = λ
solution.explanation: The first dark direction of a single slit satisfies a sin θ = λ. With θ = 30° the slit width is twice the wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.65 µm takes a = λ (θ = 90°). 2.6 µm uses a sin θ = 2λ (the second minimum). 0.33 µm uses a sin θ = λ/2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction - the single slit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A concave mirror of focal length 1.0 m forms an image of the Sun. The Sun's disc subtends an angle of 0.5° at the mirror. The diameter of the image of the Sun is about:

solution.concept: Image of a distant object forms in the focal plane; size = f × angle (in radians)
solution.explanation: Rays from the two edges of the Sun's disc arrive as parallel beams inclined at 0.5°. Each beam focuses in the focal plane, so the image diameter is f times the angle in radians.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 mm uses the radius of curvature (2 m) instead of f. 4.4 mm halves the angle. 0.50 m uses the angle in degrees instead of radians.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an optical fibre, the core has a refractive index of 1.60 and the cladding a refractive index of 1.20. The critical angle at the core–cladding boundary is about:

solution.concept: Critical angle between two media: sin C = n_rarer/n_denser
solution.explanation: Light inside the core meets the cladding; total internal reflection needs the angle of incidence to exceed C, where sin C = n_cladding/n_core.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41° is 90° − C. 39° is the critical angle for a core–air boundary (sin C = 1/1.60). 56° is the critical angle for a cladding–air boundary (sin C = 1/1.20).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection - optical fibres

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A real object is placed on the principal axis of a thin lens of focal length f. Match the situation in List-I with the image in List-II.

List-I:
A. Convex lens, object at a distance 2f from the lens
B. Convex lens, object between the focus and the optical centre
C. Convex lens, object very far away (practically at infinity)
D. Concave lens, object at any distance

List-II:
I. Virtual, erect, magnified, on the same side as the object
II. Virtual, erect, diminished, between the optical centre and the focus on the object side
III. Real, inverted, same size, at 2f on the other side
IV. Real, inverted, highly diminished, at the focus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Images formed by thin lenses (1/v − 1/u = 1/f)
solution.explanation: For a convex lens: object at 2f → image at 2f, same size, real, inverted; object within f → virtual, erect, magnified on the object side; object at infinity → point image at F. A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image between the lens and its focus for a real object.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/C-III swaps the 2f and infinity cases. B-II/D-I swaps the convex lens (magnified) with the concave lens (diminished). C-II/D-IV gives the concave lens a real image, which it cannot form for a real object.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A ray of light passes through an equilateral glass prism (angle A = 60°). Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At minimum deviation, the angles of refraction at the two faces are equal, each being A/2.
(b) At minimum deviation, the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence.
(c) At minimum deviation, the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to the base of the prism.
(d) The angle of minimum deviation does not depend on the refractive index of the prism material.
(e) For a given prism material, the angle of minimum deviation does not depend on the angle A of the prism.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Refraction through a prism: r₁ + r₂ = A; δ = i + e − A; minimum deviation
solution.explanation: At minimum deviation the path is symmetric: i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2, so the ray inside travels parallel to the base. From n = sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2), D_m depends both on n and on A.
steps: (c) symmetric path → parallel to base: true
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c). Options with (d) or (e) are wrong because D_m depends on both n and A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A tank filled with water appears shallower than it really is when viewed from directly above.
Reason (R): Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it passes from water into air, so the rays reaching the eye appear to come from a point above the bottom.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Apparent depth due to refraction
solution.explanation: Rays from a point on the bottom refract away from the normal at the water surface (water is denser than air). Traced back, the emerging rays meet at a point above the real one, so the bottom seems raised: apparent depth = real depth/n. R is the reason for A.
steps: Water → air: ray bends away from the normal → R true
Backward extensions meet above the bottom → A true, explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the mechanism of A, so option B is wrong; both statements are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Light travels from each medium in List-I into air. Match the refractive index of the medium with the critical angle in List-II.

List-I:
A. n = 2
B. n = √2
C. n = 1.25
D. n = 2/√3

List-II:
I. 45°
II. 60°
III. 30°
IV. about 53°

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: sin C = 1/n for a medium–air boundary
solution.explanation: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray grazes the surface: sin C = 1/n. A larger n gives a smaller C.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II/D-III uses cos C = 1/n. B-IV/C-I swaps the critical angles of n = √2 and n = 1.25. C-II/D-IV swaps those of n = 1.25 and n = 2/√3; in each case a larger index would get a larger critical angle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light is incident at 45° on one refracting face of a prism of angle 75°, made of glass of refractive index √2. Which statement correctly describes what happens at the second refracting face?

options.text: The ray is totally reflected back into the prism at the second face, since the angle of incidence there exceeds the critical angle
The ray emerges at 45° to the normal, and the total deviation is 15°
The ray emerges grazing along the second face, and the total deviation is 60°
The ray emerges grazing along the second face, and the total deviation is 135°

solution.concept: Prism relations r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A; critical angle
solution.explanation: Snell's law at the first face gives r₁; then r₂ = A − r₁. Compare r₂ with the critical angle (sin C = 1/√2, C = 45°). Here r₂ equals C exactly, so the emergent ray grazes the surface (e = 90°).
solution.why_others_wrong: Total reflection would need r₂ to exceed 45°; it only equals it. Emergence at 45° wrongly takes e = r₂. A deviation of 135° forgets to subtract the prism angle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism
solution.final_answer: Option C: The ray emerges grazing along the second face, and the total deviation is 60°

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through three ideal polaroids P₁, P₂ and P₃ in that order. The pass axis of P₂ makes an angle of 30° with that of P₁, and the pass axis of P₃ is perpendicular to that of P₁. The intensity of the light emerging from P₃ is:

solution.concept: Polaroid halves unpolarised light; Malus's law I = I' cos²θ
solution.explanation: P₁ passes half of the unpolarised light. The plane-polarised light then passes P₂ (at 30°) and P₃, which is at 90° − 30° = 60° to P₂, each time reduced by cos² of the angle between successive axes.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero would be correct only without P₂ (P₁ and P₃ are crossed). 3I₀/16 forgets the factor ½ at P₁. 9I₀/32 uses 30° again for P₃ instead of 60°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin plano-convex lens of glass (refractive index 1.5) has a curved surface of radius of curvature 20 cm. Its plane surface is silvered, and light is incident on the curved surface. The system behaves as a concave mirror of focal length:

solution.concept: Silvered lens: P = 2P_lens + P_mirror
solution.explanation: Light passes through the lens, is reflected by the silvered surface and passes through the lens again, so the lens power counts twice. A plane mirror has zero power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 cm is the focal length of the lens alone. 6.7 cm is the result when the curved surface is silvered (P = 2/40 + 2/20). 10 cm is R/2 of the curved surface used as a mirror alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment can be increased by using an objective of smaller focal length, the eyepiece being unchanged.
Statement II: The magnifying power of a compound microscope increases if the focal length of its objective is increased, other things remaining unchanged.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Magnifying powers: telescope f_o/f_e; microscope (L/f_o)(D/f_e)
solution.explanation: A telescope in normal adjustment has m = f_o/f_e, so a larger, not smaller, objective focal length increases m (Statement I false). A compound microscope has m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e), so increasing f_o decreases m (Statement II false). The two instruments need opposite choices of objective.
steps: Telescope m = f_o/f_e → smaller f_o reduces m → Statement I false
Microscope m ∝ 1/f_o → larger f_o reduces m → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are false, so options A, C and D, which need at least one of them to be true, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the lower half of a convex lens is covered with an opaque sheet, the lens still forms a complete image of an object, though the image is less bright.
Reason (R): Rays from each point of the object pass through every part of the lens, and all of them are brought together at the image of that point.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Image formation by a lens: every part of the lens forms the whole image
solution.explanation: Each object point sends rays to the whole lens surface, and all these rays converge at the corresponding image point. Covering half the lens removes half of the rays from every object point, so every image point still forms but receives less light. R is the reason for A.
steps: Rays from every object point reach every part of the lens → R true
Half the lens still forms every image point, with half the light → A true and explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the reason the full image survives, so option B is wrong; both statements are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Young's double-slit experiment with monochromatic light, the waves from the two slits reach the screen with equal intensities, each I₀. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The maximum intensity on the screen is 4I₀.
(b) At a point where the phase difference between the two waves is π/2, the intensity is 2I₀.
(c) At a point where the path difference is λ/2, the intensity is 2I₀.
(d) If one slit is closed, the intensity at the position of the central bright fringe becomes I₀.
(e) The intensity averaged over many fringes is 4I₀.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Resultant intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2)
solution.explanation: For two equal coherent waves, I = I₀ + I₀ + 2I₀ cos φ = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2). It is 4I₀ at φ = 0, 2I₀ at φ = π/2 and zero at φ = π (path difference λ/2). With one slit closed, only I₀ arrives. Energy is redistributed, so the average over many fringes is 2I₀, not 4I₀.
steps: (c) Δ = λ/2 → φ = π → zero: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (d). The other options include (c) or (e), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about polarisation and polaroids are correct?

(a) A polaroid transmits only the component of the electric field of the light along its pass axis.
(b) Sound waves in air can be plane polarised by a suitable polariser.
(c) The light transmitted by a polaroid is plane polarised.
(d) When plane-polarised light falls on an ideal polaroid whose pass axis is parallel to the direction of vibration of its electric field, all the light is transmitted.
(e) Unpolarised light can be polarised by passing it through a polaroid, but never by reflection.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Polaroids; transverse nature of light; polarisation by reflection
solution.explanation: A polaroid passes the E-component along its axis, so its output is plane polarised; if the incident light is already polarised along the axis, cos²0° = 1 and all of it passes. Only transverse waves can be polarised, so sound in air (longitudinal) cannot. Light can also be polarised by reflection (completely at Brewster's angle).
steps: (b) sound in air is longitudinal → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (d). The other options include (b) or (e), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
