questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of energy 4.2 eV fall on a metal surface, and the stopping potential for the emitted photoelectrons is 1.7 V. The work function of the metal is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: hν = φ₀ + eV₀
solution.explanation: The stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy: K_max = eV₀. The rest of the photon energy is the work function.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.9 eV adds K_max to the photon energy. 1.7 eV is K_max, not the work function. 4.2 eV is the photon energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of a moving electron is 0.33 nm. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the magnitude of its momentum is:

solution.concept: de Broglie relation λ = h/p
solution.explanation: The momentum of the particle is Planck's constant divided by its de Broglie wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 × 10²³ inverts the relation (λ/h). 2.2 × 10⁻⁴³ multiplies h by λ. 2.0 × 10⁻²⁵ is a slip in the power of ten (0.33 nm = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: In his experiments of 1887 on electromagnetic waves, Hertz observed that the high-voltage sparks across the detector loop were enhanced when the emitter plate was illuminated by:

options.text: ultraviolet light from an arc lamp
radio waves from a second spark gap
red light from a filament lamp

solution.concept: Hertz's observations
solution.explanation: Hertz noticed that ultraviolet light falling on the emitter plate made it easier for sparks to pass: the light helped free charged particles (electrons) from the metal surface. This was the first observation of the photoelectric effect.
steps: Hertz (1887): UV on emitter → sparks enhanced
solution.why_others_wrong: The textbook account names ultraviolet light from an arc lamp; infrared, radio waves and red light have too little energy per photon to free electrons from the metal used.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect - Hertz's observations
solution.final_answer: Option B: ultraviolet light from an arc lamp

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 400 nm falling on a metal surface ejects photoelectrons with a stopping potential V₁; light of wavelength 300 nm on the same surface gives a stopping potential V₂. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, V₂ − V₁ is about:

solution.concept: eV₀ = hc/λ − φ₀; the work function cancels in the difference
solution.explanation: Writing Einstein's equation for both wavelengths and subtracting removes the unknown work function.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.13 V is the energy of a 300 nm photon in eV, not a difference. 0.52 V halves the answer. 12.4 V divides hc by the difference of the wavelengths, which is not how energies combine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy (both moving much slower than light). Taking the mass of the proton as 1836 times that of the electron, the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the electron to that of the proton is about:

solution.concept: λ = h/p = h/√(2mK)
solution.explanation: For equal kinetic energies, p = √(2mK) ∝ √m, so λ ∝ 1/√m. The lighter electron has the longer wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1836 is the mass ratio, not its square root (that would be the answer for equal speeds). 1/43 inverts the ratio. 1 would be the answer for equal momenta.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a photoelectric experiment, a photocurrent flows even when the collector is at zero potential with respect to the emitter.
Statement II: In the photoelectric effect, a photon gives only part of its energy to an electron and then continues with reduced energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Photocurrent at zero collector potential; photon absorption
solution.explanation: Photoelectrons leave the emitter with kinetic energies from zero up to K_max, so many reach the collector even with no accelerating potential; a retarding potential is needed to stop them (Statement I true). In the photoelectric effect the photon is absorbed completely, giving all its energy hν to one electron (Statement II false).
steps: Emitted electrons have kinetic energy → current at V = 0 → Statement I true
Photon absorbed as a whole → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false, so options A and D are wrong; Statement I is true, so option B is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', experimental study of photoelectric effect; photon picture
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about de Broglie waves are correct?

(a) The relation λ = h/p applies to every material particle in motion.
(b) For a fixed momentum, the de Broglie wavelength of a particle depends on its electric charge.
(c) The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest decreases as the accelerating potential difference is increased.
(d) An electron and a photon that have the same wavelength have the same energy.
(e) Two particles with equal momenta have equal de Broglie wavelengths, whatever their masses.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: λ = h/p; electron: λ = h/√(2meV); photon E = pc
solution.explanation: λ depends only on momentum, so equal momenta give equal wavelengths and charge plays no part once p is fixed. A larger accelerating voltage gives a larger momentum and a shorter wavelength. A photon and an electron with the same λ have the same momentum, but the photon's energy pc is much larger than the electron's p²/2m.
steps: (b) λ = h/p, charge does not enter: false
(d) same p, but E_photon = pc ≫ p²/2m: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (e). The other options include (b) or (d), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An alpha particle (mass 6.4 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C), initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its de Broglie wavelength is about:

solution.concept: Charged particle accelerated through V: K = qV, λ = h/√(2mqV)
solution.explanation: The kinetic energy gained is qV, where q is the full charge of the alpha particle (2e). Then p = √(2mK) and λ = h/p.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 × 10⁻¹² m uses the charge e instead of 2e. 2.9 × 10⁻¹² m is the value for a proton. 7.3 × 10⁻¹³ m uses a charge of 4e.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission from a metal is 500 nm. Light of wavelength 250 nm falls on it. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is:

solution.concept: Work function from the threshold wavelength: φ₀ = hc/λ₀; K_max = hc/λ − hc/λ₀
solution.explanation: At the threshold wavelength the photon energy just equals the work function. The excess energy of the shorter wavelength photon appears as K_max.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.96 eV is the photon energy. 7.44 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it. 1.24 eV halves the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a photoelectric experiment with light of fixed frequency and intensity, making the collector more and more positive with respect to the emitter eventually stops increasing the photocurrent.
Reason (R): At that stage all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter are already reaching the collector.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Saturation current
solution.explanation: The emitter releases a fixed number of electrons per second (set by the intensity). A positive collector potential draws more of them across until every emitted electron is collected; beyond that the current cannot grow, which is the saturation current. R gives the reason for A.
steps: All emitted electrons collected → current saturates → A true, R true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly why the current saturates, so option B is wrong; both are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of potential on photoelectric current
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the radius of a nucleus of mass number A as R = R₀A^(1/3), the ratio of the radius of the ²⁷Al nucleus to that of the ⁶⁴Cu nucleus is:

solution.concept: Nuclear radius R ∝ A^(1/3)
solution.explanation: R₀ cancels in the ratio, leaving the cube root of the ratio of the mass numbers.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 : 64 is the ratio of the volumes (mass numbers). 9 : 16 is the ratio of the surface areas (A^(2/3)). 4 : 3 inverts the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model the energy levels of a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number Z are E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from a He⁺ ion (Z = 2) that is in its first excited state (n = 2) is:

solution.concept: Ionisation from level n: energy = |E_n|
solution.explanation: Removing the electron takes it from E_n to zero, so the energy needed is |E_n| = 13.6 × 4/4 eV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 54.4 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state (n = 1). 3.4 eV uses Z = 1 (hydrogen). 6.8 eV uses Z instead of Z².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U contains:

solution.concept: Composition of a nucleus: Z protons and N = A − Z neutrons
solution.explanation: In the symbol ᴬ_Z X, the subscript Z is the number of protons and the superscript A is the total number of nucleons, so N = A − Z.
solution.why_others_wrong: 238 neutrons takes A as the neutron number. The other two options interchange the roles of Z and N or A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', atomic masses and composition of nucleus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For the electron in the hydrogen atom in the Bohr model, match each quantity in List-I with the way it depends on the principal quantum number n (List-II).

List-I:
A. Radius of the orbit
B. Speed of the electron
C. Magnitude of the total energy
D. Orbital angular momentum

List-II:
I. n
II. n²
III. 1/n
IV. 1/n²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bohr model: r_n ∝ n², v_n ∝ 1/n, E_n ∝ −1/n², L = nh/2π
solution.explanation: Quantising L = nh/2π with the condition for circular orbits gives r_n = n²a₀ and v_n = v₁/n, and the energy E_n = −13.6/n² eV.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/C-II swaps the radius and the energy. B-I/D-III swaps the speed and the angular momentum. C-I/D-IV gives the energy the dependence of L.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (E_n = −13.6/n² eV), the electron is in an orbit where its total energy is −1.51 eV. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its orbital angular momentum is about:

solution.concept: Identify n from E_n; then L = nh/2π
solution.explanation: The energy fixes the orbit number; Bohr's quantisation condition then gives the angular momentum.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is h/2π (n = 1). 9.45 × 10⁻³⁴ J s uses n = 9 (n² instead of n). 2.10 × 10⁻³⁴ J s uses n = 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the ratio of the time period of revolution of the electron in the ground state (n = 1) to that in the first excited state (n = 2) is:

solution.concept: T = 2πr/v with r ∝ n² and v ∝ 1/n → T ∝ n³
solution.explanation: The orbit grows as n² while the speed falls as 1/n, so the time for one revolution grows as n³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 4 uses only r ∝ n². 1 : 2 uses only v ∝ 1/n. 8 : 1 inverts the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a nuclear reaction, the total rest mass of the particles before the reaction equals their total rest mass after it.
Statement II: In a nuclear reaction, the total number of nucleons before the reaction equals the total number after it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conservation laws in nuclear reactions; mass–energy equivalence
solution.explanation: Energy released in fission or fusion comes from a decrease of rest mass, Q = (Δm)c², so rest mass is not conserved (Statement I false). The number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) is the same on both sides of a nuclear reaction (Statement II true).
steps: Q = Δm c² ≠ 0 → rest mass changes → Statement I false
Nucleon number conserved → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false, so options A and C are wrong; Statement II is true, so option B is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy; nuclear energy
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the alpha-particle scattering experiment of Geiger and Marsden, and its interpretation by Rutherford, are correct?

(a) A very thin gold foil was used as the target.
(b) The scattered alpha particles produced brief flashes of light (scintillations) on a screen, which were viewed through a microscope.
(c) The number of alpha particles scattered fell off rapidly as the angle of scattering increased.
(d) The results supported the model in which electrons are embedded in a uniform sphere of positive charge.
(e) The experiment showed that the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m to 10⁻¹⁴ m in size, very small compared with the atom.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Geiger–Marsden experiment and the nuclear model
solution.explanation: Alpha particles were directed at a thin gold foil, and the scattered ones were counted by the scintillations they produced on a screen, viewed through a microscope. Most went nearly straight through and the number fell rapidly with the scattering angle, but a few were turned through large angles. This could not be explained by Thomson's model and led to a tiny nucleus of size about 10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹⁴ m.
steps: (d) the results ruled out Thomson's model: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (e). The other options include (d), which is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle scattering and Rutherford's nuclear model of atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The fission of one ²³⁵U nucleus releases about 200 MeV of energy. Taking the mass of the nucleus as 235 u and 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the percentage of the mass of the nucleus that is converted into energy is about:

solution.concept: Mass–energy equivalence: the rest-mass energy of the nucleus is 235 × 931.5 MeV
solution.explanation: Express the mass of the nucleus as an energy and compare the energy released with it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.85% divides 200 MeV by 235 and treats the result as a percentage (it is the energy per nucleon in MeV). 9% and 0.009% are slips by factors of 100 and 10.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy - fission

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the ground state of the hydrogen atom in the Bohr model, the electron moves in a circle of radius 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m with a speed of 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the equivalent electric current due to the orbital motion of the electron is about:

solution.concept: Current of a revolving charge: I = e/T = ev/(2πr)
solution.explanation: The electron passes any point of its orbit once every period T = 2πr/v, carrying charge e each time, so the equivalent current is e/T.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.6 mA uses ev/r, leaving out 2π. 0.53 mA and 2.1 mA are off by a factor of 2 in the period.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the reaction ¹H + ⁷Li → ⁴He + ⁴He, the binding energy per nucleon is 5.60 MeV for ⁷Li and 7.07 MeV for ⁴He (the proton, a single nucleon, has no binding energy). The energy released in the reaction is about:

solution.concept: Q = (total binding energy of products) − (total binding energy of reactants)
solution.explanation: The energy released equals the increase in total binding energy. Multiply each binding energy per nucleon by the number of nucleons in that nucleus.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 MeV subtracts the binding energies per nucleon without multiplying by the nucleon numbers. 95.8 MeV adds the binding energies. 10.9 MeV is the magnitude obtained by counting only one helium nucleus, which would even make the reaction absorb energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For the Balmer series of hydrogen, given by 1/λ = R(1/2² − 1/n²), n = 3, 4, 5, ..., the ratio of the longest wavelength to the shortest wavelength in the series is:

solution.concept: Longest wavelength: n = 3 → 2; shortest (series limit): n = ∞ → 2
solution.explanation: The longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy gap (3 → 2) and the shortest from the series limit (∞ → 2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 9 inverts the ratio. 4 : 3 is the corresponding ratio for the Lyman series and 16 : 7 for the Paschen series.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The emission spectrum of hydrogen gas contains many lines, although each hydrogen atom has only one electron.
Reason (R): In a sample of hydrogen, different atoms are excited to different energy levels and make different downward transitions, each transition emitting a photon of one particular wavelength.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Origin of the many lines of the hydrogen spectrum
solution.explanation: One transition of one atom emits one photon of one wavelength. A sample contains a huge number of atoms; in a discharge they are raised to various levels and drop by various routes (e.g. 3 → 2, 3 → 1, 4 → 2, ...), so all the lines appear together. R is the reason for A.
steps: One transition → one photon of one wavelength
Many atoms, many different transitions → many lines → A true and explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R explains why one-electron atoms give many lines, so option B is wrong; both are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', line spectra of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On the basis of resistivity, solids are classified as metals, semiconductors and insulators. The resistivity of semiconductors typically lies in the range:

solution.concept: Classification of solids by resistivity
solution.explanation: Metals have resistivities of about 10⁻² to 10⁻⁸ Ω m, insulators about 10¹¹ to 10¹⁹ Ω m, and semiconductors lie in between, about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻² Ω m is the range for metals and 10¹¹ to 10¹⁹ Ω m for insulators. 10⁻¹⁹ to 10⁻¹¹ Ω m is lower than any real material.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A solar cell works on the same basic principle as a photodiode. In its construction, the junction area of a solar cell is kept much larger than that of a photodiode because:

options.text: a larger junction area increases the band gap of the semiconductor
more solar radiation must fall on the junction so that more power can be generated
a larger junction area allows the cell to be operated in reverse breakdown
a larger junction area makes the cell emit light when current is passed through it

solution.concept: Solar cell: a large-area p-n junction for photovoltaic generation
solution.explanation: A solar cell, like a photodiode, generates electron–hole pairs by light near the junction, and the junction field separates them; but it is used without external bias to supply power. Its junction area is kept large so that a large amount of solar radiation is intercepted and more power is delivered.
steps: Same principle as a photodiode (light → e–h pairs → separated by junction field)
Large area → more incident radiation → more power
solution.why_others_wrong: The band gap is a property of the material, not of the junction area. A solar cell is not operated in breakdown. Light emission under forward current is the working of an LED.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices - solar cell
solution.final_answer: Option B: more solar radiation must fall on the junction so that more power can be generated

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 6.0 V is connected in reverse bias, through a 450 Ω series resistor, to a 15 V DC supply. No load is connected across the Zener diode, which is in its breakdown region. The current through the Zener diode is:

solution.concept: Zener in breakdown holds V_Z; the series resistor drops the rest
solution.explanation: In breakdown the Zener voltage stays at 6.0 V, so the series resistor has 15 − 6 = 9 V across it. With no load, all of the current through the resistor flows through the Zener diode.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33 mA puts the whole 15 V across the resistor. 13 mA uses the Zener voltage across the resistor. 47 mA adds the two voltages.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each sample of silicon in List-I with the description of its charge carriers in List-II (n_e = number density of free electrons, n_h = number density of holes).

List-I:
A. Pure silicon at 0 K
B. Pure silicon at room temperature
C. Silicon doped with arsenic
D. Silicon doped with aluminium

List-II:
I. n_e = n_h, both non-zero
II. n_h ≫ n_e
III. No free charge carriers
IV. n_e ≫ n_h

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
solution.explanation: At 0 K no covalent bonds are broken, so pure Si has no free carriers. At room temperature thermal energy creates electron–hole pairs, so n_e = n_h. Arsenic (pentavalent) donates electrons → n-type, n_e ≫ n_h. Aluminium (trivalent) accepts electrons, creating holes → p-type, n_h ≫ n_e.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I/B-III swaps the 0 K and room-temperature cases. C-II/D-IV swaps the n-type and p-type dopants.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier using ideal diodes, the peak voltage across the whole secondary winding of the transformer (from one end to the other) is 24 V. The peak voltage across the load resistor is:

solution.concept: Centre-tap rectifier: each diode uses half of the secondary
solution.explanation: The load is connected between the centre tap and the diodes. During each half-cycle only one half of the secondary drives current through the load, so the peak load voltage is the peak voltage of half the winding.
steps: Each half of the secondary: 24/2 = 12 V peak
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 V uses the whole secondary. 17 V is the rms value of a 24 V peak, which is not asked. 6 V halves the half winding again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two silicon junction diodes are connected in series, both forward biased, with a 1.2 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V DC supply. Treating each diode as having a constant forward voltage drop of 0.7 V when it conducts, the current in the circuit is:

solution.concept: Diode forward drop; loop rule
solution.explanation: Both diodes conduct, each taking 0.7 V. The rest of the supply voltage appears across the resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.6 mA subtracts the drop of only one diode. 4.2 mA ignores both drops. 2.4 mA subtracts three drops.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal 9 V battery is connected in series with a 1 kΩ resistor and a parallel combination of an ideal junction diode and a 2 kΩ resistor. The diode is connected so that it is reverse biased by the battery. The current drawn from the battery is:

solution.concept: Ideal diode: open circuit in reverse bias, short circuit in forward bias
solution.explanation: A reverse-biased ideal diode carries no current, so the parallel branch behaves as the 2 kΩ resistor alone, in series with 1 kΩ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 mA treats the diode as conducting, shorting out the 2 kΩ resistor. 4.5 mA ignores the 1 kΩ resistor. Zero forgets that current can still flow through the 2 kΩ resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under reverse bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Silicon, with a band gap of about 1.1 eV, is a suitable material for making light emitting diodes that emit visible light.
Statement II: The colour (wavelength) of the light emitted by an LED is decided by the band gap of the semiconductor it is made of.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Light emitting diode: photon energy ≈ band gap
solution.explanation: In an LED, recombining electrons and holes emit photons of energy about E_g, so the band gap fixes the colour (Statement II true). Visible photons need about 1.8 eV to 3 eV, so the band gap must be at least about 1.8 eV; silicon's 1.1 eV is too small, and compound semiconductors such as GaAsP are used instead (Statement I false).
steps: hν ≈ E_g → band gap sets the colour → Statement II true
Visible light needs E_g ≳ 1.8 eV > 1.1 eV → Statement I false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false, so options A and C are wrong; Statement II is true, so option B is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices - light emitting diode
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each two-input gate in List-I with its outputs in List-II, listed for the inputs (A, B) = (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) in that order.

List-I:
A. AND
B. OR
C. NAND
D. NOR

List-II:
I. 1, 1, 1, 0
II. 0, 0, 0, 1
III. 1, 0, 0, 0
IV. 0, 1, 1, 1

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables: AND = A·B, OR = A + B, NAND = NOT(A·B), NOR = NOT(A + B)
solution.explanation: AND is 1 only for (1,1); OR is 0 only for (0,0); NAND and NOR are the complements of AND and OR.
solution.why_others_wrong: C-III/D-I swaps NAND and NOR. A-I/B-III gives AND and OR the outputs of NAND and NOR. B-I/C-IV swaps OR and NAND.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', logic gates
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about rectifiers are correct?

(a) A capacitor connected across the load of a rectifier reduces the ripple in the output voltage.
(b) With such a capacitor filter, a larger value of the product CR_L (capacitance × load resistance) gives a smoother output.
(c) The output of a half-wave rectifier without a filter is a steady DC voltage with no ripple.
(d) In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier, the current through the load flows in opposite directions during the two half-cycles of the input.
(e) A rectifier converts an alternating voltage into a unidirectional (pulsating) voltage.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rectification and capacitor filtering
solution.explanation: A rectifier passes current in one direction only, giving a pulsating, unidirectional output (not steady DC). A capacitor across the load charges at the peaks and discharges slowly through R_L between them; the larger the time constant CR_L, the less the voltage falls, so the smoother the output. In a full-wave rectifier the two diodes conduct alternately but both send current through the load in the same direction.
steps: (d) same direction through the load: false
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (e) only leaves out the true statement (b). The other options include (c) or (d), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 10 V is used to keep the voltage across a 1.0 kΩ load at 10 V. It is connected in parallel with the load, and the combination is joined through a series resistor R to a 15 V DC supply. For proper regulation, the current through the Zener diode must not fall below 5 mA. The largest value of R that can be used is about:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: I_R = I_L + I_Z; V_R = V_in − V_Z
solution.explanation: The load current is fixed by V_Z and R_L. The series resistor must carry the load current plus at least the minimum Zener current, with 15 − 10 = 5 V across it; a larger R would give a smaller current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 500 Ω leaves no current for the Zener (it uses I_L alone). 1000 Ω leaves out the load current. 250 Ω uses 20 mA, adding the minimum Zener current twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 6.0 V and a silicon junction diode are connected in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor across a 12 V DC supply. The Zener diode is reverse biased and in its breakdown region, and the silicon diode is forward biased with a constant drop of 0.7 V. The current in the circuit is:

solution.concept: Loop rule with a Zener in breakdown and a forward-biased diode
solution.explanation: The Zener in breakdown keeps 6.0 V across it and the silicon diode 0.7 V; the resistor takes the remainder of the 12 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.0 mA ignores the drop across the silicon diode. 6.7 mA adds that drop instead of subtracting it. 11.3 mA ignores the Zener voltage, as if the Zener were forward biased with no drop.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At room temperature, pure silicon is a much poorer conductor of electricity than copper.
Reason (R): The number density of free charge carriers in pure silicon at room temperature (about 10¹⁶ m⁻³) is far smaller than the number density of free electrons in copper (about 10²⁹ m⁻³).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Carrier concentration and conductivity
solution.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. In copper essentially every atom contributes a free electron (about 10²⁹ m⁻³), while in pure silicon only a tiny fraction of bonds is broken at room temperature (n_i about 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³). This huge difference in carrier density is why silicon conducts so much worse. R explains A.
steps: n(Cu) ~ 10²⁹ m⁻³ vs n_i(Si) ~ 10¹⁶ m⁻³ → R true
Far fewer carriers → much higher resistivity → A true and explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the cause of A, so option B is wrong; both are true, so options C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic semiconductor
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A Zener diode voltage regulator consists of a series resistor and a Zener diode, in reverse breakdown, connected in parallel with a fixed load resistor. The input voltage is increased slightly, the Zener diode remaining in breakdown. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The current through the series resistor increases.
(b) The current through the Zener diode increases.
(c) The voltage across the load remains practically constant.
(d) The current through the load increases appreciably.
(e) The voltage across the series resistor remains unchanged.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Zener regulation: I_R = I_Z + I_L with V_Z constant
solution.explanation: In breakdown the Zener voltage, and hence the load voltage and load current, stay practically constant. The extra input voltage appears across the series resistor, so its voltage and current rise, and the extra current flows through the Zener diode.
steps: V_R = V_in − V_Z rises → (e) false, (a) true
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (b). The other options include (d) or (e), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment to find the figure of merit of a galvanometer, a current of 60 µA through it produces a steady deflection of 30 divisions. The figure of merit of the galvanometer is:

solution.concept: Figure of merit = current per unit deflection
solution.explanation: The figure of merit is the current needed to produce a deflection of one division: k = I/θ.
steps: k = 60 µA/30 divisions = 2 µA per division
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 µA per division inverts the ratio (that is divisions per µA). 60 µA per division ignores the number of divisions. 1800 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: While plotting the reverse-bias characteristic of a p-n junction diode, the reverse current is measured with a microammeter rather than a milliammeter because:

options.text: the reverse current is very large, beyond the range of a milliammeter
the reverse current is very small, of the order of microamperes
a milliammeter cannot be connected in a reverse-biased circuit
the reverse current flows only after breakdown

solution.concept: Reverse saturation current of a junction diode
solution.explanation: Under reverse bias only minority carriers cross the junction, so the current is tiny (µA range) and nearly constant until breakdown. A milliammeter would show practically no deflection.
solution.why_others_wrong: The reverse current is very small, not very large. Any ammeter can be connected in series in reverse bias. A small reverse current flows before breakdown too.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under reverse bias
solution.final_answer: Option B: the reverse current is very small, of the order of microamperes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The screw of a screw gauge advances by 2.0 mm in 4 complete rotations, and its circular scale has 100 equal divisions. There is no zero error. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the main scale reading is 3.5 mm and the 27th division of the circular scale is on the reference line. The diameter of the wire is:

solution.concept: Pitch = distance per rotation; least count = pitch/number of circular divisions
solution.explanation: First find the pitch from the given advance, then the least count, then add the circular-scale contribution to the main scale reading.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.770 mm takes the least count as 0.01 mm (pitch 1 mm). 4.040 mm takes the pitch as 2.0 mm. 3.527 mm takes the least count as 0.001 mm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In Searle's experiment, a load of 4.0 kg produces an extension of 0.50 mm in a wire of length 2.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. Taking g = 10 m/s², the Young's modulus of the material of the wire is about:

solution.concept: Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(Δl/L) = FL/(πr²Δl)
solution.explanation: The stretching force is the weight of the load. The area uses the radius, half of the measured diameter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.1 × 10¹⁰ uses the diameter as the radius. 8.2 × 10¹¹ uses half the radius. 2.0 × 10⁸ leaves the extension in millimetres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment on viscosity, a steel ball of radius 1 mm falling through a viscous liquid attains a terminal velocity of 2 cm/s. Another steel ball of radius 2 mm, made of the same steel, falls through the same liquid. Assuming Stokes' law holds, its terminal velocity is:

solution.concept: Terminal velocity v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η) ∝ r²
solution.explanation: For the same materials and liquid, everything in the terminal-velocity formula is fixed except r², so doubling the radius makes v four times larger.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 cm/s takes v ∝ r. 16 cm/s takes v ∝ r³ (the weight alone). 1 cm/s makes the larger ball slower.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity - Stokes' law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a simple pendulum experiment, the effective length is measured as 100.0 cm with an accuracy of 0.1 cm, and the time for 100 oscillations is measured as 200 s with a stop-watch of resolution 1 s. The maximum percentage error in the value of g obtained from g = 4π²L/T² is:

solution.concept: Error propagation: Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2ΔT/T
solution.explanation: The fractional error in the period equals that in the total time measured (T = t/100 → ΔT/T = Δt/t). Because T appears squared, its fractional error counts twice.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6% forgets the factor 2 for T². 0.7% puts the factor 2 on L instead of T. 1.0% leaves out the error in L.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In each experiment of List-I, a straight-line graph is plotted. Match the experiment with the quantity obtained from the graph (List-II).

List-I:
A. Simple pendulum: T² plotted against the effective length
B. Verification of Ohm's law: potential difference plotted against current
C. Searle's apparatus: extension plotted against the load
D. Convex lens by the u–v method: 1/v plotted against 1/u (magnitudes)

List-II:
I. Focal length, from the intercepts on the axes
II. Resistance, from the slope
III. Acceleration due to gravity, from the slope
IV. Young's modulus, from the slope

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Using straight-line graphs in laboratory experiments
solution.explanation: T² = (4π²/g)L, so the slope gives g. V = RI, so the slope gives R. Extension = (L/AY) × weight, so the slope gives Y. For a convex lens with magnitudes, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, so both intercepts equal 1/f.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/C-III swaps the pendulum and Searle's experiment. B-I/D-II swaps the lens and Ohm's law. A-I/D-III gives the lens graph the pendulum's quantity.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I
